The advanced tech is almost uncontrollable and cybersecurity analysts need to learn how it can be utilized responsibly. Employee training and development of enterprise tools would strengthen cybersecurity procedures until an industry giant like Microsoft uses Security Copilot to transform the industry. In the meantime, companies must stop sticking their head in the sand hoping for reality to change.
Things will become more dystopian if organizations continue to ignore rampant problems instead of dealing with the uncomfortable world we’ve created.

title: Inside the secret list of websites that make AI chatbots sound smart
text:
Inside the secret list of websites that make AI chatbots sound smart
AI chatbots have exploded in popularity over the past four months, stunning the public with their awesome abilities, from writing sophisticated term papers to holding unnervingly lucid conversations.
Chatbots cannot think like humans: They do not actually understand what they say. They can mimic human speech because the artificial intelligence that powers them has ingested a gargantuan amount of text, mostly scraped from the internet.
[Big Tech was moving cautiously on AI. Then came ChatGPT.]
This text is the AI’s main source of information about the world as it is being built, and it influences how it responds to users. If it aces the bar exam, for example, it’s probably because its training data included thousands of LSAT practice sites.
Tech companies have grown secretive about what they feed the AI. So The Washington Post set out to analyze one of these data sets to fully reveal the types of proprietary, personal, and often offensive websites that go into an AI’s training data.
To look inside this black box, we analyzed Google’s C4 data set, a massive snapshot of the contents of 15 million websites that have been used to instruct some high-profile English-language AIs, called large language models, including Google’s T5 and Facebook’s LLaMA.
The Post worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI on this investigation and categorized the websites using data from SimilarWeb, a web analytics company. About a third of the websites could not be categorized, mostly because they no longer appear on the internet. Those are not shown.
Tap on the boxes above to view top sites
We then ranked the remaining 10 million websites based on how many “tokens” appeared from each in the data set. Tokens are small bits of text used to process disorganized information — typically a word or phrase.
Wikipedia to Wowhead
The data set was dominated by websites from industries including journalism, entertainment, software development, medicine and content creation, helping to explain why these fields may be threatened by the new wave of artificial intelligence. The three biggest sites were patents.google.com No. 1, which contains text from patents issued around the world; wikipedia.org No. 2, the free online encyclopedia; and scribd.com No. 3, a subscription-only digital library. Also high on the list: b-ok.org No. 190, a notorious market for pirated e-books that has since been seized by the U.S. Justice Department. At least 27 other sites identified by the U.S. government as markets for piracy and counterfeits were present in the data set.
Some top sites seemed arbitrary, like wowhead.com No. 181, a World of Warcraft player forum; thriveglobal.com No. 175, a product for beating burnout founded by Arianna Huffington; and at least 10 sites that sell dumpsters, including dumpsteroid.com No. 183, that no longer appear accessible.
Others raised significant privacy concerns. Two sites in the top 100, coloradovoters.info No. 40 and flvoters.com No. 73, had privately hosted copies of state voter registration databases. Though voter data is public, the models could use this personal information in unknown ways.
Content without consent
Top Business & Industrial sites:
fool.com
kickstarter.com
sec.gov
marketwired.com
city-data.com
myemail.constantcontact.com
finance.yahoo.com
prweb.com
entrepreneur.com
globalresearch.ca
Business and industrial websites made up the biggest category (16 percent of categorized tokens), led by fool.com No. 13, which provides investment advice. Not far behind were kickstarter.com No. 25, which lets users crowdfund for creative projects, and further down the list, patreon.com No. 2,398, which helps creators collect monthly fees from subscribers for exclusive content.
Kickstarter and Patreon may give the AI access to artists’ ideas and marketing copy, raising concerns the technology may copy this work in suggestions to users. Currently, artists receive no compensation or credit when their work is included in AI training data, and they have lodged copyright infringement claims against text-to-image generators Stable Diffusion, MidJourney and DeviantArt.
The Post’s analysis suggests more legal challenges may be on the way: The copyright symbol — which denotes a work registered as intellectual property — appears more than 200 million times in the C4 data set.
All the news
Top News sites:
nytimes.com
latimes.com
theguardian.com
forbes.com
huffpost.com
washingtonpost.com
businessinsider.com
chicagotribune.com
theatlantic.com
aljazeera.com
The News and Media category ranks third across categories. But half of the top 10 sites overall were news outlets: nytimes.com No. 4, latimes.com No. 6, theguardian.com No. 7, forbes.com No. 8, and huffpost.com No. 9. (Washingtonpost.com No. 11 was close behind.) Like artists and creators, some news organizations have criticized tech companies for using their content without authorization or compensation.
Meanwhile, we found several media outlets that rank low on NewsGuard’s independent scale for trustworthiness: RT.com No. 65, the Russian state-backed propaganda site; breitbart.com No. 159, a well-known source for far-right news and opinion; and vdare.com No. 993, an anti-immigration site that has been associated with white supremacy.
Chatbots have been shown to confidently share incorrect information, but don’t always offer citations. Untrustworthy training data could lead it to spread bias, propaganda and misinformation — without the user being able to trace it to the original source.
Religious sites reflect a Western perspective
Top Religious sites:
patheos.com
gty.org
jewishworldreview.com
thekingdomcollective.com
biblehub.com
liveprayer.com
lds.org
wacriswell.com
wdtprs.com
bibleforums.org
Sites devoted to community made up about 5 percent of categorized content, with religion dominating that category. Among the top 20 religious sites, 14 were Christian, two were Jewish and one was Muslim, one was Mormon, one was Jehovah’s Witness, and one celebrated all religions.
The top Christian site, Grace to You (gty.org No. 164), belongs to Grace Community Church, an evangelical megachurch in California. Christianity Today recently reported that the church counseled women to “continue to submit” to abusive fathers and husbands and to avoid reporting them to authorities.
The highest ranked Jewish site was jewishworldreview.com No. 366, an online magazine for Orthodox Jews. In December, it published an article about Hanukkah that blamed the rise of antisemitism in the United States on “the far-right, fundamentalist Islam,” as well as “an African-American community influenced by the Black Lives Matter movement.”
Anti-Muslim bias has emerged as a problem in some language models. For example, a study published in the journal Nature found that OpenAI’s ChatGPT-3 completed the phrase “Two muslims walked into a …” with violent actions 66 percent of the time.
A trove of personal blogs
Top Technology sites:
instructables.com
ipfs.io
docs.microsoft.com
forums.macrumors.com
medium.com
makeuseof.com
sites.google.com
slideshare.net
s3.amazonaws.com
pcworld.com
Technology is the second largest category, making up 15 percent of categorized tokens. This includes many platforms for building websites, like sites.google.com No. 85, which hosts pages for everything from a Judo club in Reading England to a Catholic preschool in New Jersey.
The data set contained more than half a million personal blogs, representing 3.8 percent of categorized tokens. Publishing platform medium.com No. 46 was the fifth largest technology site and hosts tens of thousands of blogs under its domain. Our tally includes blogs written on platforms like WordPress, Tumblr, Blogspot and Live Journal.
These online diaries ranged from professional to personal, like a blog called “Grumpy Rumblings,” co-written by two anonymous academics, one of whom recently wrote about how their partner’s unemployment affected the couple’s taxes. One of the top blogs offered advice for live-action role-playing games. Another top site, Uprooted Palestinians, often writes about “Zionist terrorism” and “the Zionist ideology.”
Social networks like Facebook and Twitter — the heart of the modern web — prohibit scraping, which means most data sets used to train AI cannot access them. Tech giants like Facebook and Google that are sitting on mammoth troves of conversational data have not been clear about how personal user information may be used to train AI models that are used internally or sold as products.
What the filters missed
Like most companies, Google heavily filtered the data before feeding it to the AI. (C4 stands for Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus.). In addition to removing gibberish and duplicate text, the company used the open source “List of Dirty, Naughty, Obscene, and Otherwise Bad Words,” which includes 402 terms in English and one emoji (a hand making a common but obscene gesture). Companies typically use high-quality datasets to fine-tune models, shielding users from some unwanted content.
While this kind of blocklist is intended to limit a model’s exposure to racial slurs and obscenities as it’s being trained, it also has been shown to eliminate some nonsexual LGBTQ content. As prior research has shown, a lot gets past the filters. We found hundreds of examples of pornographic websites and more than 72,000 instances of “swastika,” one of the banned terms from the list.
Meanwhile, The Post found that the filters failed to remove some troubling content, including the white supremacist site stormfront.org No. 27,505, the anti-trans site kiwifarms.net No. 378,986, and 4chan.org No. 4,339,889, the anonymous message board known for organizing targeted harassment campaigns against individuals.
We also found threepercentpatriots.com No. 8,788,836, a downed site espousing an anti-government ideology shared by people charged in connection with the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. And sites promoting conspiracy theories, including the far-right QAnon phenomenon and “pizzagate,” the false claim that a D.C. pizza joint was a front for pedophiles, were also present.
Is your website training AI?
A web crawl may sound like a copy of the entire internet, but it’s just a snapshot, capturing content from a sampling of webpages at a particular moment in time. C4 began as a scrape performed in April 2019 by the nonprofit CommonCrawl, a popular resource for AI models. CommonCrawl told The Post that it tries to prioritize the most important and reputable sites, but does not try to avoid licensed or copyrighted content.
The websites in Google’s C4 dataset

|---|
1 of 0
The Post believes it is important to present the complete contents of the data fed into AI models, which promise to govern many aspects of modern life. Some websites in this data set contain highly offensive language and we have attempted to mask these words. Objectionable content may remain.
Note: Some websites were unable to to be categorized and, in many cases, are no longer accessible.
While C4 is huge, large language models probably use even more gargantuan data sets, experts said. For example, the training data for OpenAI’s GPT-3, released in 2020, began with as much as 40 times the amount of web scraped data in C4. GPT-3’s training data also includes all of English language Wikipedia, a collection of free novels by unpublished authors frequently used by Big Tech companies and a compilation of text from links highly rated by Reddit users. (Reddit, a site regularly used in AI training models, announced Tuesday it plans to charge companies for such access.)
[Quiz: Did AI make this? Test your knowledge.]
Experts say many companies do not document the contents of their training data — even internally — for fear of finding personal information about identifiable individuals, copyrighted material and other data grabbed without consent.
As companies stress the challenges of explaining how chatbots make decisions, this is one area where executives have the power to be transparent.

title: Council Post: How AI Will Revolutionize The Future Of SEO
text:

The foundation of search engines like Google relies on sophisticated algorithms that crawl and index webpages, and then rank them based on their relevance and authority. AI-powered algorithms have the potential to vastly improve these processes, making search results more accurate, personalized and efficient.
One example of AI integration in search algorithms is Google’s RankBrain, which uses machine learning to better understand user intent and deliver more relevant search results. As AI becomes more advanced, we can expect search engines to adopt similar technologies, leading to a more accurate understanding of user queries and better search results.
Improved Keyword Research And Content Optimization
Keyword research and content optimization are crucial aspects of SEO. AI can help automate and improve these tasks, including understanding the semantic relationships between keywords, identifying search trends and predicting user behavior.
AI-powered tools can also assist in optimizing content, ensuring it is relevant and engaging for users. By analyzing user behavior, AI can determine the best-performing content and provide recommendations to improve it. Furthermore, AI can help generate meta tags, headings and other on-page elements that are crucial for SEO success.
Enhanced User Experience
User experience plays a critical role in SEO, as search engines prioritize websites that offer a seamless experience to their users. AI can help improve user experience by analyzing user behavior data, identifying areas of improvement and suggesting personalized content.
For example, AI can analyze user preferences and deliver personalized content recommendations, ensuring that users find what they are looking for and stay on the website longer. Additionally, AI-powered chatbots can provide instant assistance to visitors, improving customer satisfaction and engagement.
Predictive SEO
Predictive SEO is a concept that involves using AI to forecast future trends, user behavior and search engine algorithm updates. By leveraging AI and machine learning, businesses can stay ahead of the curve, anticipating changes and adapting their SEO strategies accordingly.
Predictive SEO can help businesses identify trending topics and create content that appeals to their target audience. Additionally, it can help businesses detect potential algorithm updates and adjust their strategies to minimize the impact on their rankings.
Voice Search Optimization
The rise of voice assistants like Amazon’s Alexa, Apple’s Siri and Google Assistant has led to a significant increase in voice search queries. As AI becomes more advanced, voice recognition technology will continue to improve, making voice search an essential aspect of SEO.
To optimize for voice search, businesses will need to focus on natural language processing and long-tail keywords. AI can help analyze voice search queries, understand user intent and provide insights into how businesses can optimize their content for voice search.
Visual Search Optimization
Visual search is another area where AI will have a significant impact. Platforms like Google Lens and Pinterest Lens enable users to search for products and information using images instead of text. AI-powered image recognition technology can identify objects within images, making it easier for search engines to understand and index visual content.
To capitalize on visual search, businesses will need to optimize their images with relevant metadata and ensure that their website’s visual content is easily accessible. AI can help analyze and optimize images, making it easier for search engines to index them and improving the chances of ranking in visual search results.
Conclusion
AI is undoubtedly poised to revolutionize the future of SEO. From AI-powered search algorithms to improving keyword research and content optimization, businesses will benefit from a more accurate, personalized and efficient SEO landscape. The advancements in AI technology also promise to enhance user experience, predictive SEO, voice search optimization and visual search optimization, further transforming the way businesses optimize their online presence.
To stay ahead of the curve, businesses must embrace these changes and adapt their SEO strategies to leverage the benefits that AI brings. By harnessing the power of AI, businesses can ensure they remain competitive in the ever-evolving digital landscape and continue to deliver a seamless, engaging experience for their users. As we move forward, the integration of AI in SEO will become increasingly important, shaping the future of search and online visibility.

title: Council Post: A New Era For Content Creation: 4 Strategies To Leverage AI In Your Digital Asset Management
text:
Sebastien is the VP Sales North America of Wedia, a provider of an Enterprise Digital Asset Management (DAM) solution.
In one Heinz advertising campaign, the company chose to get creative and employ the help of the Gen-AI tool, DALL-E 2, to prove that Heinz really is the go-to sauce. When the AI tool was asked to summon up a ketchup bottle, it churned out multiple examples of a Heinz one.
In a turn of clever strategic messaging, of course, the results were not accidental. Indeed, the generative-AI (Gen-AI) platform had been practicing, having been trained on hundreds of bottles of Heinz ketchup to make sure that it recognized this type of ketchup ahead of any others.
AI tools are certainly rising in prominence, and the recent buzz surrounding ChatGPT has only succeeded in making them a talking point across the world. From rewriting Nick Cave songs to debugging code, AI has a lot to offer.
In this article, I will outline three strategies for leaders on how to best implement DAM and AI solutions within their marketing and communication.
1. Digital Asset Management and AI
Digital Asset Management (DAM) refers to powerful tools leveraged by companies across the world to manage their content requirements. As a disclosure, my company Wedia is one provider of such solutions. As communication and marketing specialists keep up with the rising need for greater amounts of content—across multiple platforms and channels—the need to stock, share and track various assets has become essential.
A DAM solution allows media formats such as videos, images and audio files to be stored in one centralized hub, meaning assets can be shared easily and quickly between internal and external stakeholders. The tool’s abilities don’t stop there, though, as a DAM system can be plugged into other software such as a Content Management System (CMS) or Product Information Management (PIM), and users can track their content across multiple platforms to give them a fully-rounded vision of their campaigns and projects.
DAM systems have not escaped the pull of AI, and in fact, AI and DAM are beginning to establish a solid and innovative partnership.
2. Managing Significant Volumes Of Assets With Meta Tags
For large, multibrand, multilocation companies, the number of assets stored in a DAM platform can run into the thousands, millions or even billions. In order for marketing and communications teams to pull a specific photo or video from the DAM environment, it needs to be tagged with the relevant information, including keywords and descriptions.
When this task is carried out by humans with such large volumes of assets, there is room for error. Spelling mistakes, slight differences in how assets are classed (United Kingdom vs. the U.K., for example) can lead to the right assets not appearing in search terms.
Leaders opting to hand this job over to AI within the DAM solution should focus on finding ways to better mitigate the risk of human error. Thanks to image recognition, automated tagging and metadata management, AI can class and organize assets in a way that makes them easy to find for users of the DAM platform.
3. Gen-AI: Creating Images That Don’t Yet Exist
Gen-AI is a sub-branch of AI that involves the creation of content from video to music and photography. Take, for example, American artist August Kamp, who used OpenAI’s DALL-E software to build the space outside of Johannes Vermee’s famous painting, "Girl With A Pearl Earring." Using aspects such as textures, colors and reflections from the original painting, the AI constructed an imagined version of the surroundings around the girl.
This kind of AI technology can also be used within a DAM environment by marketing and communications teams for a multitude of reasons.
For example, a marketing team looking to brief a creative agency for a campaign related to the release of a new product can generate images from within the DAM solution and provide a mood board of inspiration for the designers.
Rather than relying on descriptions, in-house teams can more precisely brief agencies in order to accurately describe the results they are expecting. By working off written language, users can input text prompts into the Gen-AI, which then creates new images for them. Typing in "coke bottle in space," for example, may leave you with images ranging from a bottle on the moon to one flying across a starry sky.
4. Other Applications For Product Content
Another way to use Gen-AI in a DAM platform is through the creation of simple but effective product content for social media campaigns or to update existing photoshoots. Let's say a confectionary brand releases a new product, for example, and the social media team wants to play around with the product in different locations: under the sea, in the desert or even during the ice age. These kinds of imagined scenarios can be generated from the DAM tool and then shared directly to a brand’s social media, and the results tracked.
By using a DAM system as a multi-functional tool, it becomes more than a content repository but a one-stop shop for content creation, storage and tracking.
The Future DAM And AI Applications
I hope this article provides some valuable takeaways for leaders seeking strategies to best leverage AI within their operations. By finding the strategic use cases best suited to their purposes, leaders will be best positioned to leverage this technology to its most fully realized potential.

title: Council Post: Which Problems Are Enterprises Trying To Solve With Generative AI?
text:
Assaf Baciu is cofounder and COO at Persado, a generative AI-for-marketing platform trusted by some of the world's largest brands.
In the two years since OpenAI commercialized the GPT-3 large language model (LLM), the buzz surrounding generative AI has focused on individual knowledge workers increasing their output. That was partly a result of the ease with which even non-technical users could sign up for Jasper.ai or, more recently, ChatGPT and test the technology.
However, the conversation is shifting. Beyond shadow IT adoption by individual business users, corporate leaders are asking how their teams can leverage generative AI for the enterprise and how to identify the right generative AI provider.
There are pitfalls to using ChatGPT or other LLM-generated languages out of the box with little human oversight. Frankly, AI can lie. Generative AI used in an enterprise context must be accurate. Many data scientists are working on mitigating AI hallucinations and misinformation by fine-tuning LLMs to focus on specific tasks or fields or specifying prompts to narrow a model's focus. This might minimize the accuracy issues and give enterprises the confidence to adopt LLMs.
If your organization has already taken the leap, the chances of realizing returns can improve if you approach the technology with clarity about which of two enterprise problems you're trying to solve.
Generative AI Works Through Prediction
LLMs fall into the category of AI known as natural language processing (NLP). They can process natural language "data" (spoken or written), understand its intent or context and generate relevant outputs.
However, while those outputs often look and sound like there is true intelligence behind them, there isn't. Generative AI tools built on LLMs don't understand what they've read—at least not in the way that humans do. Instead, LLMs identify and codify patterns based on datasets comprising millions of sentences in their training data. When later prompted to generate an output, whether a marketing email or poem, the result (simply put) is based on predictions of what the next likely words are—or, in the case of image generators, what an image of a dog or an avocado looks like.
Two Types Of Problems Generative AI Is Primed To Solve
The ability of LLMs to correctly predict words and, in turn, craft original content is so vast that there are countless challenges generative AI can help solve right now. Those challenges fall under two broad categories: efficiency and effectiveness.
Solving Efficiency Challenges
Efficiency challenges pertain to creating enough of whatever output you're trying to produce at an affordable price point. Efficiency challenges are problems of scale, and every function in an organization deals with some version of them.
Much of the discussion around generative AI has focused on opportunities for marketing teams to more efficiently create websites, emails, ads, social campaigns and content marketing assets, to name a few. Organizations' content generation needs don't stop with marketing, however. Product teams need product descriptions, technical documentation and disclaimers. Investor relations teams need quarterly reports and roadshow presentations. Legal and compliance need regulatory reporting. IT needs application code.
Those are just a few of the outputs that explicitly rely on language. While LLMs are best known for generating language and visuals based on language prompts, the potential enterprise use cases span much further.
For example, there are healthcare organizations building LLMs based on health record data. Generative AI dedicated to the health space could help doctors update records more efficiently or even identify new molecules or treatment options. Parallel activity is underway in R&D, as some manufacturers are leveraging LLMs in the ideation phase of product design.
Solving Effectiveness Challenges
Effectiveness is about producing outputs that are better in terms of the results you're trying to achieve. Whereas efficiency aims for quantity, effectiveness targets quality.
In marketing, for example, more ads or email marketing messages can be counterproductive if they're irrelevant to a customer's needs or speak to them too generically. More, in this case, is likely to produce brand fatigue, a phenomenon where the customer tunes out and stops seeing a brand's messages. Instead of efficiency, brands would achieve greater impact with marketing that is more effective at engaging customers and motivating conversion.
Effectiveness challenges also appear in every context in which the enterprise produces ideas. Effective investor relations messages can attract stockholders. Effective talent recruitment can increase your ability to attract new high-potential employees. Effective customer service can build brand loyalty.
Effectiveness also applies to innovation. Looking again at the healthcare example, an LLM that is more efficient at generating new ideas for medical intervention won't necessarily improve health outcomes. Generating more effective ideas, however, has the potential to produce more treatment options more quickly—resulting in fewer failed medical experiments and leading to more positive patient outcomes.
Efficiency Matters, Effectiveness Transforms
Generative AI is already proving to be useful for solving efficiency problems (i.e., generating a lot of content quickly). That's where most of the attention has focused, for good reason. GPT-3, the best-known LLM and the only one that is commercially available at low cost, is an out-of-the-box efficiency tool—in part because it was trained to be broadly useful rather than specialized and is, therefore, too general on its own to reliably address more specific or nuanced problems.
However, the arc of generative AI's enterprise evolution is trending toward effectiveness as businesses look for competitive advantages by leveraging AI to transform how they operate. For generative AI to deliver effective outputs and predictive models, the out-of-the-box functionality available through the GPT-3 API won't be good enough.
Enterprise generative AI requires more advanced capabilities in the form of either specialized models trained on real-world data relevant to the problem or fine-tuned models, knowledge bases containing insights, problem-centric prompts and other techniques to produce effective outputs at scale. Businesses that tap into this specialization should be able to both reduce the risk of AI that can "hallucinate" and increase business impact.
