title: Amid Growing Call To Pause AI Research, LAION Petitions Governments To Keep AGI Research Open, Active And Responsible
text:
Few outside of the AI Research Community have heard of LAION, a large-scale Artificial Intelligence Open Network, with an aim to democratize access to large-scale machine learning models, datasets and related code. Their recent petition calling for a CERN-like global organization to coordinate efforts on the transparency of large-scale AI research outside of Big Tech giants, has been in direct response to the controversial open letter that called for an immediate moratorium on AI for at least 6 months.
The call to pause AI research for at least 6 months has amassed over 30,000 signatures, as of this writing, including renowned members of the academic community, top researchers and Big Tech including Amazon, CAIDP, Pinterest, Apple, and MILA. Eliezer Yudkowsky, a lead researcher for the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, alarmingly called to “Shut it All Down” writing,
“If somebody builds a too-powerful AI, under present conditions, I expect that every single member of the human species and all biological life on Earth dies shortly thereafter.”
Disturbed by the unrestrained growth of AI’s Large Language Models (LLMs) and the constant media attention to the troubling model outcomes, advocates for this Open Letter, originating from the Future of Life have warned of the real potential that anyone can exploit AI to achieve goals that counter the existing moral, ethical and societal norms. The immediate pause has called for independent review and regulation before it’s too late.
Initiated by the founding members, the LAION petition offered a much different perspective, specifically calling out the grave implications if humanity is to solely rely on Big Tech to take on the responsibility of advancing artificial intelligence technology that remains opaque and impenetrable, and driven by profit motives. In their petition, the group proclaimed,
“To harness their full potential as tools for societal betterment, it is vital to democratize research on these models and to access them, lest we face severe repercussions for our collective future.”
The petition calls on governments of US, UK, EU, AU and Canada and interested governments to establish an international, publicly funded open-source supercomputing research facility, equipped with at least 100,000 high performance state-of-the-art accelerators operated by the ML experts within the supercomputing research community with oversight by elected institutions among the participating countries.
I spoke with LAION’s Cofounders: Christoph Schuhmann, an educator and computer scientist who oversees a community of thousands of scientists, developers and engineers united by a common goal to make state-of-the-art AI models truly open; and Jenia Jitsev, Deep Learning and Computational Neuroscience researcher, Lab leader at Juelich Supercomputing Center (JSC), Helmholtz Association, and Cofounder of LAION; as well as Irina Rish, Full Professor in the Computer Science and Operations Research Department at the Université de Montréal (UdeM), and a core member of Mila - Quebec AI Institute; and Huu Nguyen, an active volunteer for LAION and Cofounder of Ontocord.AI, a startup focusing on responsible AI –– to understand their own motivations in developing this petition.
Schuhmann spent the last 10 years advising over 50 startup groups for innovative private schools where children are free to unfold their curiosity and study what they are interested in. He recalls the moment the petition came out,
“When we saw the petition for the Future of Life Institute, we surmised that no matter how many people would sign this, in the end, Big Tech like Microsoft (MS), Open AI or Google would not care very much about it. They will continue with efforts to advance the technology. Those who will listen and who fear the consequences whether they be researchers, academic labs, or from industry will be paralyzed and this will lead to an even stronger monopolization of this technology at the benefit of the big players.”
While Schuhmann maintains he does not believe MS or Google have bad motivations, the reality is that, at the moment, every request to GPT3 and GPT4 runs through the Open AI API. The implication for one or two APIs for all is a grave one, as Schuhmann points out,
“This basically means that the whole world will soon have MS Office products integrated with GPT4, and the same for Google’s BARD… And all the data of the entire world would basically go through a few APIs. Governments and businesses will become completely dependent on the technologies coming from the largest companies who have invested millions, and by definition have the highest objective to profit from it.”
In the weeks following the call for a moratorium on AI experiments, Google’s race to protect its search domination has been threatened by Microsoft’s integration of AI into Bing search engine. Microsoft also plans to add its ChatGPT-like AI to its Office Products. Let’s add Linkedin, the largest professional network’s announcement (also owned by Microsoft) to roll out government issued-ID and employment email to verify user identity and employment of its 875 million users. And if anyone has questioned Elon Musk’s seemingly altruistic motives in signing the earlier petition, his recent announcement to launch a rival AI to Open AI quickly surfaced his true intentions. This increasing dependence that Schuhmann describes is already in the making:
“If you are a member of the public sector, an educator, a not for profit, who are dependent upon organizations that do not have the public good as their primary objective, then this is scary. The second reason why we launched this petition is for security and the safety of research which currently is completely impossible to perform any transparent safety research unless you have access to the [model] weights. Researchers do not have access to the model behind the API, whether it gets updated or if a benchmark dependent on the API is arbitrarily switched off.”
What LAION is calling for is the distribution of transparent, fair and safe research that would be public and accessible to the scientific community and the general public. This would not only spark billions of startup innovations, but it would also mitigate much of the negative impacts of bias, harmful manipulation, job displacement, etc. Schuhmann believes that the alarmist intentions conveyed by the signatories of the Open Letter are pessimistic and sometimes over-exaggerated,
“The vast majority of people want to lead a normal life. So, if the majority of actors in an economy have a vital interest in some kind of stability, simply by open sourcing a foundational model, the internet would not instantly collapse. In fact, the opposite would probably take place. The scientific community in many private security companies and institutions would instantly adapt and improve the general security because they could use these tools to fight cybercrime and mitigate cyber risks.”
He emphasizes the wakeup call to the general public, to the scientific communities, universities and to the politicians and decision makers that they need to make an enormous effort to catch up so that in two years when we have arrived at versions GPT5 or GPT6 that quickly will also exist an open-source version of it. The immediate danger, otherwise, as Schuhmann puts it, is the monopolization of power over the whole global knowledge work:
“I do not question Microsoft’s intentions and they have been doing great work in the open-source community but this is simply the nature of the game – the scenario to centralize power behind API’s to, as one journalist I spoke to said: one API to rule them all and one API to bind them.”
David Ha, Engineer of Stability AI, former Goldman Sachs, and former Research Scientist at Google Brain, who supports the LAION petition, also disagrees with the sky-is-falling mentality:
“Machine learning models are not going to “take over” and eradicate humanity. But rather, just like all technologies before, humans will simply adapt to them, and absorb the new technology into our everyday lives, making these models part of our collective intelligence… That these models will integrate into our everyday lives is precisely why we need open ML that is not controlled by a centralized party. The “AGI Doomer” fear-mongering narrative distracts from actual dangers, implicitly advocating for centralized control and power consolidation.”
Jenia Jitsev obtained his PhD in computer science at the Frankfurt Institute for Advanced Studies (FIAS) and the University Frankfurt, working on plasticity and unsupervised learning in recurrent hierarchical neural networks of the visual cortex, with applications to object and face recognition. He stresses that the broader the research community that is involved in studying these models, the better the research quality and the safer it will become for the public. He agrees there are risks bound to a technology becoming public and how to mitigate them is to allow for big scale research:
“The big scale research means there are expert-driven research safety labs that we also propose in our petition to be part of the international AI research facility, tightly coupled to the basic and applied research on large-scale AI and equipped with enough compute resources to dig into those… that would make sure that there are anticipatory research and measures… developed to mitigate the most plausible risk scenarios. Without it we are doomed and indeed any actor with enough resources, can grab the current state of technology and develop it in the dark. To avoid this situation, you need big scale research that involves experts from the broad research community to assess all plausible scenarios and develop countermeasures that will respond appropriately. Such countermeasures can also lead to powerful AI systems that are specifically developed to supervise and enforce safety of activities from AI models and tools already active or to be deployed.”
Irina Rish is also a member of LAION. She holds a Canada Excellence Research Chair (CERC) in Autonomous AI and a Canadian Institute for Advanced Research (CIFAR) Canada AI Chair and she sums up the work she is doing with open-source communities like LAION, EleutherAI and Together.xyz in this way:
“AI field is progressing at unprecedented speed; however, training state-of-art AI models such as GPT-4 requires large compute resources, not currently available to researchers in academia and open-source communities; the ‘compute gap’ keeps widening, causing the concentration of AI power at a few large companies. This motivated us – a rapidly growing international collaboration across several Universities and non-profit organizations – to join forces and initiate an effort towards developing common objectives and tools for advancing the field of large-scale foundation models, and obtaining large-scale compute funded by either governments (e.g., supercomputers such as JUWELS in Germany, Jean Zay in France, Summit in USA, etc.) or private entities (e.g., stability.ai). For example, we are currently able to train relatively large (up to 20B) models thanks to the INCITE program award we obtained on the Summit supercomputer at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility (OLCF).
We believe that making state-of-art, powerful AI open-source will help to achieve AI democratization, as opposed to concentrating the power in hand of several companies. Our long-term, overarching goal is to develop a wide international collaboration united by the objective of building foundation models that are increasingly more powerful, while at the same time are safe, robust and aligned with human values. Such models aim to serve as the basis for numerous AI applications, from industry to healthcare to scientific discovery - i.e., AI-powered applications of great societal value. ”
The other side of progress and safety involves the deployment of the technology into the public domain. This is much harder and more complicated to distribute, which means this must be done in tandem with governments when it comes to infrastructure, and coordinated with policy.
For LAION, which aggregates much of the data for LLMs and develops open models, this petition represents a bigger movement – of people from academia, the tech industry, students – united in a broader community who have a shared dream of open source and donating their time. Schuhmann adds,
“There are many people who join our server or other communities like Eleuther AI, and the more powerful technologies like ChatGPT become, the more people understand that it is important to make open-source versions of them. And I don’t think one specific organization will be the savior of democracy. This is a shakeup to the public and hopefully the politicians in US and EU… so they understand there needs to be an international effort to provide open science and evolve the scientific community as an open, inclusive community that has meant to keep pace with innovation.”
Jitsev emphasizes that LAION does not want to compete with ChatGPT. The goal is to create an infrastructure funded by different nations, organizations, and actors to change the way we do research and achieve technological innovations that will make developments as ChatGPT a cumulative win for research and society:
“There is a win/win for everyone when you create an environment of transparent research that includes open-sourcing foundational tools and models, while collectively using the safety labs to do proper, transparent research on safety aspects. Once this is done, only then should determinations be made about the potential risks. This means establishing scientific consensus on the varying levels of danger and establishing proper security access levels. Such studies will be conducted in virtual sandboxes for AI systems with high risk potential. What you then bring to the public will have been checked and decided by the broad scientific community consensus.”
This, compared to what we see today are rules, which are largely dictated, without transparency, by one or two companies.
On establishing guardrails as these models are developed, there needs to be implicit trust by the user community that even in open source, how we define bias, how we call out anomalies in models that may fit objectives but may still need some “attention” is nuanced. There are very few standards that integrate some of the moral or social contexts when these models are built. How are values defined and what controls need to be in place to ensure they are addressed when reviewing model outcomes?
Huu Nguyen, who co-led the data governance efforts for BigScience and founded the Legal, Privacy and Ethics working group for Big Science, established the importance of context:
“It’s different to different people. Safety cannot be defined by Open AI or Microsoft. Safety is contextual to society, to a country, to a local context. In the US, our sense of safety is very different because we can talk about hate speech. In Germany this is illegal. It must be contextual and without doing that in the open, without knowing what’s going on in the models, we don’t know how it’s working. Eventually it will cause harm immediately, and downstream. Anyone could be doing something illegal while they’re using it. So, it has to be open so that we, as scientists and as society can examine them and put those controls in place… We don’t want to have cars without seatbelts. And having seatbelts should not be a competitive advantage. It should be a RIGHT to keep people safe.”
Schuhmann added that within a given system, we will have the ability to functionally align models to existing laws but these, too, should be part of the subject of research happening in a much larger scale than what is currently exists.
He also stressed the importance of risk mitigation is to empower the public to become so resilient and capable of filtering unwanted content or experiences from their applications, or news feeds.
“These LLMs are very powerful already, and they can be used to create fake news, compose hate speech… However, I am convinced what we are experiencing right now is the last moment in human history where most of the content on the internet is created by humans. In the next few years if you go and scrape the internet, most of the content will be generated content, text, images, videos etc. And if you try to fight this you will end up with a complete surveillance state, shutting down companies or bombing data centres.( Eliezer Yudkowsky).”
He suggests giving people tools like LAION’s Open Clip Models for zero-shot detection of positive content or undesired content. This could ameliorate the tsunami of fake news or manipulative content, completely driven by the individual user. Schuhmann believes that, with all new technology, policies will follow to review and regulate safety for such tools before they’re installed on devices. This could be highly personalized and could effectively distribute the power and control in the hands of each person.
What is clear is that regulation will be difficult to keep pace with what is currently happening today. Current privacy laws regarding consent are outdated when it comes to the collection of data from large language models. And while the EU GDPR is the most robust, it struggles to be in lock step with generative models. Jitsev argues that the large-scale research will work with governments directly to combat any current harmful outcomes of models, also making use of advances in AI to create powerful systems that can assist safety research and safety measures This cannot be done in isolation. He also adds the future is a much more personalized agent that allows individuals to exercise greater control, in the process:
“It would be like a personal agent navigating in the flood of myriads of information, and by this time the brain is unable to cope with this level of data. We will evolve into a society that will rely on these powerful tools to help us work efficiently within these new environments. When it comes to consent, you could identify research directions that would give rise to the tools that treat every piece of data produced as raw material with credentials as origins that either lead to people or other systems that produce the data or verify the data. This will all become part of an infrastructure where every piece of data has a value and it is properly monetized from the individual’s preference. In essence, individuals are able to signal consent for their data in an easy and transparent way.”
What Jitsev describes is already happening within the privacy movement of the Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) Community and the use of verifiable credentials.
Nguyen summed up the LAION’s motivation in this way:
“There are disparities in education, in society and now technology. LAION is the largest human rights organization focused on equalizing data and knowledge in the world. This is in keeping with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights which every nation has agreed to. This is what the petition is focusing on. In the less developed nations around the world, they will be unable to pay $20 a month for ChatGPT. That’s not going to happen.
We need to ensure that those resources are open so that people can have basic information so that they can develop their lives in a productive way and be part of society. We are already seeing the effects of those disparities in wealth within society and between countries.
Let’s not exacerbate it with super AI controlled only by a handful of large corporations in closed-sourced ways!”
Tim Berners-Lee sounded this same alarm in 2019:
The increasing centralization of the Web has ended up producing—with no deliberate action of the people who designed the platform—a large-scale emergent phenomenon which is anti-human.”
The AI Race has effectively allowed Microsoft to surpass its tech rivals and has made it, once again, a powerful force. Microsoft’s recent announcement to bring its LLM to its Office Products indeed reveals that the price of progress using the centralized model is failing all of us. Pausing progress gives Big Tech a momentary reprieve but may do nothing to stall the inevitable. LAION’s solution, while ambitious, is the only way to distribute control and power among the masses and away from the elite few.
LAION continues to collect signatures for their Petition.
Prominent signatories from the research and tech community include:
Thomas Wolf, Cofounder and CSO Hugging Face. BigScience:
“Making sure artificial intelligence is developed in the open, in an auditable way and involving as many stakeholders as possible is the challenge of our time. More than the destination, the journey is essential to make sure this technology will be as beneficial as possible. LAION's call is a key step in this direction, and I strongly support it.”
Julien Chaumond, CTO Hugging Face:
“At Hugging Face, we want state-of-the-art Artificial Intelligence to be built by as many people as possible, not just a few large companies. Hence, I support LAION's call for public institutions to significantly invest in infrastructure for AI, for the community to build ML in the open.”
Surya Ganguli United States / California / Santa Clara M.A Mathematics, M.A Physics, PhD Theoretical Physics UC Berkeley, Assistant Professor Stanford (Department Applied Physics, Neurobiology, Electrical Engineering) , NeurIPS 2014, 2022 Outstanding Paper Award
Kristian Kersting TU Darmstadt, Director Hessian AI, Kristian Kersting is a Full Professor (W3) at the Computer Science Department of the TU Darmstadt University, Germany. He is the head of the Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AIML) lab, a member of the Centre for Cognitive Science, a faculty of the ELLIS Unit Darmstadt, and the founding co-director of the Hessian Center for Artificial Intelligence

title: The viral new 'Drake' and 'Weeknd' song is not what it seems | CNN Business
text:
One of the buzziest songs recently circulating on TikTok and climbing the Spotify charts featured the familiar voices of best-selling artists Drake and the Weeknd. But there’s a twist: Drake and the Weeknd appear to have had nothing to do with it.
The viral track, “Heart on my Sleeve,” comes from an anonymous TikTok user named Ghostwriter977, who claims to have used artificial intelligence to generate the voices of Drake and the Weeknd for the track.
“I was a ghostwriter for years and got paid close to nothing just for major labels to profit,” Ghostwriter977 wrote in the video comments. “The future is here.”
“Heart on my Sleeve” racked up more than 11 million views across several videos in just a few days and was streamed on Spotify hundreds of thousands of times. The original TikTok video has seemingly been taken down, and the song has since been removed from streaming services including YouTube, Apple Music and Spotify. (TikTok, YouTube, Apple and Spotify did not respond to a request for comment.)
The exact origin of the song remains unclear, and some have suggested it could be a publicity stunt. But the stunning traction for “Heart on my Sleeve” may only add to the anxiety inside the music industry as it goes on offense against the possible threat posed by a new crop of increasingly powerful AI tools on the market.
Universal Music Group, the music label that represents Drake, The Weeknd and numerous other superstars, sent urgent letters in April to streaming platforms, including Spotify and Apple Music, asking them to block AI platforms from training on the melodies and lyrics of their copywritten songs.
“The training of generative AI using our artists’ music — which represents both a breach of our agreements and a violation of copyright law as well as the availability of infringing content created with generative AI on digital service providers – begs the question as to which side of history all stakeholders in the music ecosystem want to be on: the side of artists, fans and human creative expression, or on the side of deep fakes, fraud and denying artists their due compensation,” the company said in a statement this week to CNN.
The record label said platforms have “a fundamental legal and ethical responsibility to prevent the use of their services in ways that harm artists.”
But attempting to crack down on AI-generated music may pose a unique challenge. The legal landscape for AI work remains unclear, the tools to create it are widely accessible and social media makes it easier than ever to distribute it.
An unknown creator and powerful AI tools
AI-generated music is not new. Taryn Southern’s debut song “Break Free,” which was composed and produced with AI, hit the Top 100 radio charts back in 2018, and VAVA, an AI music artist (i.e. not a human), currently has a single out in Thailand.
But a new crop of AI tools have made it easier than ever to quickly generate convincing images, audio, video and written work. Some services such as Boomy specifically leverage generative AI to make music creation more accessible.
There’s little known about who is behind the Ghostwriter977 account, or which tools the creator used to make the track. The user did not respond to a CNN request for comment.
In the bio section of the user’s TikTok account, a link directs users to a page on Laylo, a website where fans can sign up to get notifications from artists when new songs are dropped or merchandise and tickets become available. The company told CNN the account likely registered to build up its fan base and brought in “tens of thousands” of signups in the past few days.
Laylo CEO Alec Ellin denied that the company was behind the viral track as some have speculated, but Ellin told CNN whoever did make it was “clearly a really savvy creator” and called it “a perfect example of the power of using Laylo to own your audience.”
Michael Inouye, an analyst at ABI Research, said “Heart on my Sleeve” could have been made in several ways depending on the sophistication of the AI and level of musical talent.
“If music artists were involved, they could create the background music and the lyrics, and then the AI model could be trained with content from Drake and The Weekend to replicate their voices and singing styles,” he said. “AI could also have generated most of the song, lyrics and replicated the artists again based on the training data set and any prompts given to direct the AI model.”
He added that part of this fascination and virality of the song comes from “just how good AI has gotten at creating content, which includes replicating famous people.”
Roberto Nickson, who is building an AI platform to help boost productivity and work flow, recently posted a video on Twitter showing how easy it is to record a verse and train an AI model to replace his vocals. He used the artist formerly known as Kanye West as an example.
“The results will blow your mind,” he said. “You’re going to be listening to songs by your favorite artist that are completely indistinguishable and you’re not going to know if it’s them or not.”
The legal impact
Although the entertainment industry has seen these issues coming, regulations are lagging behind the rapid pace of AI development.
Audrey Benoualid, an entertainment lawyer based in Los Angeles, said one could argue “Heart On My Sleeve” does not infringe copyright as it appears to be an “original” composition.
“Ghostwriter also publicized that Drake and The Weeknd were not involved in the making of the song, which could protect them from a ‘passing off’ claim, where profits are generated as consumers are misled into believing the song is actually a Drake-Weeknd collaboration,” she said in an email to CNN.
However, Benoualid added, machine learning and generative AI programs may also be found to infringe copyright in existing works, either by making copies of those works to train the AI or by generating outputs that are substantially similar to those existing works. “Major labels would undoubtedly, and have already begun to, argue that their copyrights (and their artists’ intellectual property rights) are being infringed,” she said.
Michael Nash, an executive VP at Universal Music Group, recently wrote in an op-ed that AI music is “diluting the market, making original creations harder to find, and violating artists’ legal rights to compensation from their work.”
No regulations exist that dictate on what AI can and cannot train. But last month, in response to individuals looking to seek copyright for AI-generated works, the US Copyright Office released new guidance around how to register literary, musical, and artistic works made with AI.
The copyright will be determined on a case-by-case basis, the guidance continued, based on how the AI tool operates and how it was used to create the final piece or work. The US Copyright Office announced it will also be seeking public input on how the law should apply to copywritten works the AI trains on, and how the office should treat those works.
“AI and copyright law and the rights of musicians and labels have crashed into one another (once again), and it will take time for the dust to settle,” Benoualid said. “The landscape is anything but clear at the moment.”
Inouye said if AI generated content becomes associated with famous individuals in a negative way that could be grounds for a lawsuit to not only take content down but to cease and desist their operations and potentially seek damage.
“On the flip side, if the content were to be popular and the creator were to make revenue off of the artists’ image or likeness then again the artists could similarly request the content to be taken down and potentially sue for any monetary gains,” he said.
But for now, concerned parties may be forced to play whack-a-mole. While services like Spotify pulled “Heart on my Sleeve,” versions of it appeared to continue circulating as of Tuesday on other online platforms.
Even a song made with artificial intelligence may find real staying power online.
– CNN’s Vanessa Yurkevich contributed to this report.

title: Council Post: B2B Marketing In 2023: Three Trends To Watch
text:
Founder of PRNEWS.IO, an Ad-tech & PR platform for SMBs around the world.
We are currently facing global economic uncertainty. Speaking in numbers, 64% of adults in the United States are anxious about the possibility of a recession. Changing market conditions affect consumers and "the new normal" made shoppers upgrade their experiences. Since then, we've seen new ways of living, shopping and interacting. Here's what we can expect from business-to-business marketing and buying as we continue further into 2023:
Personalization will continue to be key.
In 2023, I expect personalized marketing efforts will remain popular, and B2B companies will need to leverage data to better understand their audience and deliver personalized content and experiences that appeal to them. To achieve this, companies can adopt various strategies to use data effectively, but in general, the core steps are as follows:
- Collect and analyze customer data.
- Use marketing automation tools.
- Create targeted content.
- Personalize messaging.
One example of a company that is currently doing this well is Spotify. Spotify uses data to create personalized playlists for each user based on user data such as listening history, playlists and search queries. These playlists are customized to the individual's musical tastes and are constantly updated to represent their changing preferences. Discover Weekly and Daily Mix, for example, further personalize the listening experience by exposing users to new music based on their listening habits.
AI and automation will be more prevalent (and require more oversight).
The growing use of AI and automation in marketing has shown great promise for creating more efficient and effective campaigns. The recent ban on ChatGPT in Italy, on the other hand, has highlighted the possible risks and challenges involved with these technologies.
The main reason for the ban was concerns about the confidentiality of personal information belonging to Italian citizens. According to the regulatory authority, there is "no legal basis to justify the massive collection and storage of personal data." This case highlights the importance of transparency and accountability in the collection and use of personal data in AI and automation. While these technologies can help companies create more personalized and engaging marketing experiences, it is essential that they are used responsibly and ethically.
However, these are not the only risks and challenges connected with the use of AI and automation in marketing. The effectiveness of AI algorithms is proportional to the quality of the material with which they are trained. If the data is skewed in any manner, the AI algorithm will be skewed as well. This can result in unintentional discrimination and bias. While AI and automation can be helpful tools, businesses must be careful not to overuse them. Human judgment and creativity are still important components of effective marketing efforts.
Despite the potential risks and challenges associated with AI, many companies continue to invest in these technologies to improve their marketing efforts. One example is Salesforce.
Einstein, Salesforce's AI-powered marketing platform, aims to assist companies in more effectively targeting customers. Einstein can spot trends and predict future behavior by analyzing customer data, enabling businesses to develop targeted marketing campaigns that are more likely to convert. Personalized suggestions, predictive analytics and automated workflows are among the features available.
Furthermore, Salesforce's AI tools can help automate marketing processes like lead scoring and lead nurturing, giving marketers more time to focus on strategy and innovation. This allows businesses to optimize their marketing efforts and produce better results, which can lead to increased revenue and customer engagement.
Companies can harness the full potential of AI and automation to create more efficient and effective B2B marketing campaigns by adopting a responsible and ethical approach to data collection and use.
Customer experience will become a major focus.
Customer experience plays a critical role in influencing customer loyalty and retention. To meet the expectations of customers for a seamless and personalized experience across all touchpoints, companies must invest in creating a great customer experience. Those that can deliver on these expectations are more likely to be chosen by customers, generating repeat business. To improve customer experience, companies should:
- Identify opportunities to improve the experience at each stage of the customer journey.
- Listen to feedback from surveys, reviews and social media.
- Regularly train employees on how to provide excellent customer service.
In B2B, Adobe is recognized for prioritizing customer experience with its suite of marketing and analytics tools. These tools help businesses deliver personalized experiences to customers, such as tailored emails, website content, targeted ads and social media campaigns. Adobe Target, for instance, allows businesses to run A/B tests and deliver personalized content for specific customer segments, while Adobe Analytics helps businesses track and analyze customer behavior across all channels and touchpoints. This provides businesses with insights into customer preferences and behaviors, enabling them to develop more personalized experiences.
The future of B2B marketing is likely to be shaped by a range of emerging technologies and trends that enable companies to create more personalized, engaging and sustainable experiences for customers. Stay ahead of the competition by keeping an eye on the trends.

title: Council Post: Exploring The Security Risks Of Generative AI
text:
Chief Security Advisor at Microsoft.
As forward-thinking enterprises embrace generative AI technologies to boost the effectiveness of work operations and results, they must also consider emerging security threats. According to the results of a recent Salesforce survey, 71% of 500 senior IT leaders postulate that generative AI is likely to “introduce new security risks to data.”
Commenting on the challenges of generative AI, Sam Altman, OpenAI cofounder, characterized it as “incredibly limited, but good enough at some things to create a misleading impression of greatness.” Furthermore, Atlman strongly urges companies not to utilize ChatGPT for essential tasks. In this vein, multiple renowned companies, including JPMorgan, prohibit the usage of ChatGPT (paywall) in the workplace. And other companies like Amazon and Walmart have warned the staff to "exercise caution" while utilizing AI services.
Uncovering Emerging Security Risks
As chatbots regularly gather personal data, concerns regarding data privacy have surfaced. Considering ChatGPT's privacy policy, it appears the platform collects crucial user data such as IP address, browser information and browsing activities across various websites, which might be shared with third-party entities. Wayne Sadin, CEO and board advisor of Acceleration Economy, outlines that “there’s a heightened chance of that data being broadcast far more widely to an audience that includes 'your competitors, your customers, your regulators, your board members.'”
Furthermore, AI generation provides a novel extension of the entire attack surface, introducing new attack vectors that hackers may exploit. Through generative AI, attackers may generate new and complex types of malware, phishing schemes and other cyber dangers that can avoid conventional protection measures. Such assaults may have significant repercussions like data breaches, financial losses and reputational risks.
To effectively collaborate with security leaders, businesses must approach the partnership through a risk-focused lens and carefully consider the following questions.
• What are the potential risks associated with using generative AI in our organization, and how can we mitigate those risks?
• How can we ensure that our employees are trained on the safe and responsible use of generative AI? How can we ensure that the results of generative AI are neither malevolent nor fraudulent?
• How can we monitor the generative AI system for unusual patterns or behavior that might signal security breaches?
• How can we ensure that the generative AI system complies with industry-specific requirements and data privacy laws?
How To Tackle Security Risks
In the context of the widespread adoption of generative AI, all enterprises must adopt a proactive and comprehensive approach to cybersecurity due to the evolving and sophisticated nature of cyber threats.
One viable avenue is to adopt zero-trust platforms that use anomaly detection instead of traditional antivirus software. This shift enhances threat detection and mitigation, thereby minimizing cybersecurity breaches. It's also feasible to implement checks and balances in their processes to detect and eliminate any fraudulent content. Those that rely solely on automated processes are vulnerable to cyberattacks, but a comprehensive strategy that includes human oversight can help safeguard against potential threats.
Companies that understand the risks associated with this novel technological iteration should prioritize enhancing their data loss protection controls at their endpoints and perimeter to safeguard their digital assets effectively, considering these three aspects.
1. Processes: To mitigate these risks, companies should embed controls into their model-building processes and allocate sufficient resources to ensure that their models comply with the highest levels of security regulations.
2. Governance: Governance frameworks are needed to manage AI projects, tools and teams to minimize risk and ensure compliance with various standards. Data governance, in particular, is a critical area to get right as privacy concerns mount and transparency in data collection grows in importance.
3. Ethics: Ethical considerations must be embedded in business operations to minimize bias and ensure the technology is used for ethical purposes. Neglecting ethical considerations can introduce unintended biases into the data, resulting in discriminatory AI products.
Partnering With Security Leaders To Combat Security Risks
Some businesses have rigid and inefficient methods for allocating time, money and personnel to cost-center operations like cybersecurity. Hence, internal responses may not rise to the occasion until the threats become more evident. This is why companies may want to consider working closely with security leaders to tackle these security risks to ensure a risk-focused approach. This includes identifying potential risks associated with generative AI and developing measures to mitigate those risks. Training employees on the safe and responsible use of generative AI is also crucial, as well as ensuring that the results are neither malevolent nor fraudulent.

title: Council Post: Fighting Technology Fire With Fire
text:
CEO of NTT Research, leading research in physics & informatics, cryptography & information security and medical & health informatics.
Technology gives, and technology takes away, as the saying goes. We enjoy modern communications and digital infrastructure but are concerned about cyberattacks, loss of privacy, bias, energy consumption and more. Some combinations—like surveillance cameras and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven facial recognition—seem especially threatening and scary.
What’s the right way to maximize the pros while minimizing the cons? One tactic is for industries and governments to set limits. Another approach is to fight technology with more and better technology.
Limits And Innovation
Setting limits is important. One example is the White House’s proposed AI Bill of Rights. Industries can also engage in self-regulation, but cyber criminals and other bad actors routinely flout laws and agreements. Regulations should, moreover, try to avoid inhibiting innovation.
Quantum computing, AI and other techno-genies can grant a lot of good wishes, but there’s no practical way to put them back into the bottle. Innovators will continue to invent. In many cases, they will also find solutions to the very problems that technology has created. It’s a little like fighting fire with fire.
AI And Quantum Computing
Cybersecurity offers a case in point. Security experts believe that machine learning (ML) is becoming a critical element of security information and event management (SIEM) platforms, which store and analyze information regarding threats. With cyberattackers exploiting automated software bots, enterprises can counter by tapping into ML to bolster their defenses, identify attacks and respond faster than any human security analyst can.
Quantum computing is a related example. The fear is that, sometime down the road, a fault-tolerant quantum computer will be used to break existing cryptosystems. It’s a scary prospect, but as I noted in a previous article, the race is on. Post-quantum cryptography has become a common topic at many academic conferences. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) is creating new standards, and commercial solutions are emerging.
Energy consumption is also a concern. For example, the computational requirements of deep neural networks, which is pervasive in running AI technologies today, are very concerning from the viewpoint of energy consumption. One way to address the inefficiencies of digital circuitry is to reimagine and demonstrate computing as a physical process, as some physicists have recently done. It’s potentially much more energy efficient.
As for other threats posed by AI, regulators are beginning to act. There is the proposed AI Bill of Rights mentioned above, as well as the European Union (EU)’s AI Act, which is expected to become law in 2023. Two of the five principles in the U.S. document involve algorithmic discrimination and data privacy. As in other cases, we can address these concerns through both limits and technological enablers.
Addressing Privacy And Bias
One way to prevent AI from displaying bias is to stop developing applications that do so. Over the past few years, several large tech companies, including Meta, have either gotten out of facial recognition or limited their involvement. One policy suggestion is to allow consumers to opt out of AI-driven applications. Having said that, opting out would be hard to implement, partially because that would mean walking away from the potential of otherwise useful and effective solutions.
When deployed, video surveillance combined with facial recognition software raises questions of bias and privacy. Here, too, new technologies offer possible solutions. In a recently conducted hackathon that my company hosted, the winning demo used a combination of attribute-based encryption (ABE) and ML to blur out all faces in a closed-circuit television (CCTV) feed while allowing fine-tuned control of encrypted visual data to authorized users.
As it happens, the winning team was from Belgium, where such an application would have been helpful in a metro station incident that occurred a year ago in which a woman was pushed onto the tracks. The idea is to protect the privacy of victims and bystanders while helping authorities, assuming all appropriate anti-bias protections are in place, to apprehend someone seen committing a crime.
A larger issue now is how to distinguish real versus fake, or how to correct biased AI. Given the enormous attention and powerful potential (good and bad) that ChatGPT has received lately, people are realizing we do not have an effective method to do these tasks. We are now at the stage where we are looking for such technologies.
Between Hope And Fear
Technology can spur both hope and fear. If "techlash" is indeed growing, then anxiety is also on the rise. New laws and regulations are likely to follow.
Meanwhile, it’s helpful to recall the dynamic nature of science and technology. Working in basic research, I know that progress is uneven and may require long-time horizons to materialize. But problem solvers, as a rule, aim for upgrades, not downgrades. And solutions to technical challenges often lie within the technologies themselves.

title: How Generative AI Is Forcing Changes In B2B Content
text:
The development of generative AI is showing up in everything, everywhere, all at once. From GPT-4’s arrival to the announcement of generative AI tools coming to Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and three major CRM solutions, the AI news cycle just won’t stop. For B2B marketers, it increases the pressure to define the usage of generative AI in their organization. With its promise of 10x the productivity and creative possibilities, generative AI capabilities give rise to questions such as:
- How do we use AI to create quality content at scale?
- How does this change the way that our teams work?
- If every company creates AI-generated content, how do we stand out with our audiences?
Most organizations face bottlenecks in content production. Marketers know firsthand that their organizations need to improve collaboration and efficiency in this regard. In Forrester’s 2022 State Of B2B Content Survey, 65% of B2B marketers said that their organizations struggle with significant content waste. It’s time that marketers figure this out as they’re called to do more with less in 2023 and are adjusting to ongoing scrutiny of budgets and headcount. Generative AI holds appeal for efficiency in content creation. But more importantly, for organizations committed to advancing their content engine maturity, generative AI forces a major turning point for stepping up content operations and driving alignment on content quality and innovation across the enterprise.
Plan For Enterprise AI And Content
This is a recurring theme in the B2B world, with the best marketing, product, and sales teams joining forces to power growth. This theme continues with generative AI adoption, because these teams all create, store, and activate content with audiences everywhere. Although individuals or single teams may experiment with a variety of AI tools, keeping track of dozens of different tools across an organization creates an untenable burden. Instead, innovative B2B organizations are piloting and using generative AI platforms that can be brought into the workflows that their teams use.
Successful B2B adoption calls for content expertise and marketing savvy. Content marketers and brand, communications, and portfolio marketing experts are critical for incorporating brand voice, style guidelines, and company knowledge into generative AI tools. Their expertise and partnership with marketing operations to fine-tune workflows enhances cross-functional coordination and collaboration. Although a pilot program may start within one team or function, generative AI’s enormous potential has to be managed like an enterprisewide application, with attention to security and privacy features and governance around content processes.
Use Generative AI Across The Content Lifecycle
So does this change the way that B2B teams work? Most early adopters see benefits in using generative AI as a thought starter, writing prompt, or research tool. Having an audience-centric focus and the content operations capabilities to manage and measure content utilization and performance is critical for curbing content waste. That’s where marketers can guide the organization on specific activities across the content lifecycle and drive improvements in quality and scale while the organization learns.
Generative AI takes some time in terms of onboarding and setting up templates. As team members gain more experience, they get better at writing prompts and iterating on outputs more effectively. AI can help with summarization and transcription, providing content-brief-like input and generating raw drafts and meta descriptions — but marketers stay involved, editing and refining content for quality and providing unique input, whether that’s data points and quotes or perspective from company experts. In the longer term, more marketers will use generative AI to repurpose content into different formats and promote it for different audiences.
Adapt Your Content Strategy For Future Relevance
The reality for B2B audiences is that they are saturated in content — and that’s before the widespread use of generative AI. When every organization has crossed the chasm, audiences will recognize and appreciate content that shows human qualities (empathy, humor, and emotion) and that demonstrates source accuracy and credibility. Marketers who guide their organization’s editorial perspective on this will be invaluable — and will lead their content and marketing strategies well.

title: Opinion | AI could hasten the extinction of languages — and ways of thinking
text:
Viorica Marian is director of the Bilingualism and Psycholinguistics Research Lab at Northwestern University and author of “The Power of Language: How the Codes We Use to Think, Speak, and Live Transform Our Minds.”
Far fewer. There is reason to believe that these tools could bring about a mass extinction of languages. And that, more worryingly, would expunge a diversity of ways of thinking and creating.
How this might happen holds clues for how it could be stopped.
First, some basics: Large language models (LLMs) are trained to make predictions about the best fit for what to generate next in a conversation or piece of writing. They learn that the most likely word after “bacon and” is “eggs” and that the probability of “eggs” being correct is higher if other preceding words included “breakfast” or “coffee.”
Except we are already far past bacon and eggs, and much closer to a Joël Robuchon menu combining all the offerings from his restaurants with 32 Michelin stars total. And each new iteration of LLMs surpasses the last more and more quickly.
AI language models are trained on enormous amounts of data — from the books, journals, newspapers and online content available. The more data, the better. But what’s available to train a model varies widely across the thousands of languages used today.
The most powerful models will be those trained on about 20 “high-resource languages” such as English, Mandarin, Russian, German and Japanese. In turn, AI will churn out massive amounts of new text mostly in those languages. Like invasive species, such dominant models could drive out languages for which fewer resources exist for training.
Some of these languages — such as Hawaiian, Quechua and Potawatomi — are already critically endangered because of globalization, migration and cultural homogenization. Currently, about nine per year snuff out. LLMs could increase that extinction rate dramatically.
Crucially, this is about much more than language. If a majority of languages die in the space of a few generations, that will also bring about a collapse of ways of thinking and being. Because the interaction between language and the mind is a two-way street.
Language shapes the brain. It is one of the most powerful ways to organize, process and structure information. The languages we use influence how we perceive the world, what we remember, the decisions we make, the emotions we feel and the insights we have.
In experiments in my lab at Northwestern University and others, we see that people who speak different languages make different eye movements and have different brain activity. Different things in the environment capture their attention; their memories and interpretation of the world and of reality vary. Those who speak many languages have somewhat different neural networks activated by each.
Reality as each of us perceives it is a subjective experience. It results from how our brains combine the input from our senses with knowledge and experience. Language experience gives us a prism through which to see the universe.
The demise of languages winnows the number of prisms through which to refract the world.
Here’s an irony. When I was on sabbatical at Stanford University, most Silicon Valley AI scientists I met spoke, studied, grew up with or were exposed to more than one language. Many spoke two or more languages. The very people potentially contributing to the demise of the multilingual mind are those harnessing its prowess to build these extraordinary artificial intelligence software programs.
If our reality becomes filtered through a much more limited linguistic set, shaped largely by the symbolic systems of math, logic and artificial languages, could our thinking change?
One insight comes from a version of the classic dilemma used to study morality. A trolley is speeding toward five workmen who cannot see it; you are standing on a footbridge above a train track next to a person. If you push them onto the tracks below, they will die. But they will also stop the trolley, saving the five workmen. What to do?
When responding in a native language, 20 percent of people opt to sacrifice one person to save five. Responding in a second language, 33 percent do so. This 13 percent shift toward utilitarian decision-making is called the foreign language effect.
But just when new brain imaging and computational science are beginning to give us insight into why the multilingual mind works the way it does, we are setting a course that might eliminate one of its core features.
What can be done?
Two things. First, AI research, development and use should be regulated in the public interest. At a minimum, this should be at a level similar to other private-sector industries. Better still would be a level akin to that of the defense sector.
Second, to buy time to come up with more solutions, it is imperative to keep as many natural languages actively engaging human minds for as long as possible.
Now is not the moment to reduce the supply of new ideas. Our many languages are one of the most powerful sources of diversity of thought. In the human experience, multilingualism is not noise, it is the signal.

title: Atlassian taps OpenAI to make its collaboration software smarter
text:
Atlassian on Wednesday said it will draw on technology from startup OpenAI to add artificial intelligence features to a slew of the collaboration software company's programs.
Several software companies have been mobilizing to capitalize on interest in a category called generative AI — where machines can react to human input with information informed by loads of previous data — ever since OpenAI's ChatGPT bot went viral last year with its ability to give human-like responses to written commands.
OpenAI's GPT-4 large language model, which been trained on extensive sources of text from the internet, will help Atlassian's Jira Service Management process employees' tech support inquiries in Slack. For example, an employee could type an inquiry about getting approval to view a file and the chatbot will make that possible, freeing up service agents for more challenging requests.
In Atlassian's Confluence collaboration program, workers will be able to click on terms they don't recognize in documents and find automatically generated explanations and links to relevant documents. They will also be able to type in questions and receive automated answers based on information stored in documents.
Atlassian has been building its own AI models for several years, but just started using OpenAI at the beginning of 2023. Together, these models create results that are unique to individual customers, with Atlassian's trove of data.
"We have a graph of work basically," Scott Farquhar, one of Atlassian's two founders and CEOs, told CNBC in an interview earlier this week. "I reckon we have one of the best ones in the world out there. It spans people doing stuff from design to development to test to deployment to project management to collaborating on stuff, too."
Microsoft, which is one of Atlassian's top rivals, is a large financial backer of OpenAI. Consequently, when GPT-4 responds to user input such as a request for information in a Confluence file, the underlying computing work happens in a cloud service run by Microsoft.
But Farquhar dismissed this concern, explaining that OpenAI won't be training its models on Atlassian's customer data, so Atlassian won't be necessarily making OpenAI better by giving it business.
The new features will be available under the brand Atlassian Intelligence. Customers can join a waiting list and the company will start inviting people from it over the next few months, a spokesperson said. Corporate users will only see the new features if their employers opt in.
Atlassian employees have been able to use the new Atlassian Intelligence features internally, and they have become popular, especially for those leading teams, Anu Bharadwaj, president of Atlassian, said. Bharadwaj said she appreciates the Confluence feature that lets her transform the style of content while writing it, and she finds it helpful when Atlassian Intelligence can identify the common thread across multiple products in development at the same time.
Bharadwaj said Atlassian hasn't figured out how much to charge for Atlassian Intelligence. Nor does she know how much money Atlassian will wind up paying OpenAI for GPT-4, because it isn't clear how heavily Atlassian customers will use the new features.
Farquhar said the data that companies already store in Atlassian will help its use of AI stand out.
"If you start at a company that's been using our Confluence or Jira products for 10 years, the day you start, you have access to all the information that's happened over the last 10 years," he said. That data makes for a knowledgeable "virtual teammate," he said.
In March, Microsoft's GitHub code storage subsidiary said that, thanks to a collaboration with OpenAI, it had started testing AI-generated messages to describe changes known as pull requests. GitHub said it would experiment with letting AI identify pull requests that lack software tests and suggest code for appropriate tests. Atlassian sells Bitbucket software where developers also work on pull requests. But Farquhar said Atlassian did not have any announcements about Bitbucket to discuss.
Duolingo, Morgan Stanley and Stripe are among the many companies in addition to Microsoft that have said they're integrating GPT-4.
